extracted.intended_audience: short-fiction magazine editors, submissions managers, and fiction authors interested in editorial policy around AI-generated content
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for magazine editors and submissions staff on detecting, filtering, and handling suspected AI-generated or fraudulent short fiction submissions while preserving open submissions and minimizing harm to authors. Focuses on operational processes, detector selection criteria, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-queue submissions filtering system
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are split into two queues—regular and suspicious—and reviewed by humans. Suspicious submissions are reviewed less frequently, serving as a pressure valve against surges of spam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational details: keep a regular queue for likely-valid submissions and a suspicious queue for items flagged by filters; review suspicious queue less often so spikes in spam don't overwhelm staff. If a submission is later found to be miscategorized, move it to the regular queue and use the case to improve processes to reduce false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of detected/generated submissions (ban/flag policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: If something is generated, the person is banned. If we aren’t sure, they get flagged for review on future submissions and treated like anyone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce a clear consequence (ban) for proven generated submissions. For uncertain cases, prefer flagging over immediate punitive action; track flagged authors for future scrutiny rather than immediate exclusion. Maintain records so false positives can be corrected and learning propagated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to check email/spam folders for missed submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many small magazines still accept submissions via email and have a responsibility to check those folders periodically to make sure an author’s email hasn’t been inappropriately categorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should periodically browse spam folders as a human check against automation — especially important for small publications where a miscategorized email could cost an author an opportunity. Implement periodic manual reviews as part of workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept flawed automation but require human oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are going to have to accept flawed processes that make it possible for them to do their jobs and be responsible for reviewing what gets marked as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge filters make mistakes; design workflows that combine automated filtering with human review. Use automation to reduce volume while retaining human decision-making for final judgments and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid detectors that collect submitted works for training without permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not use or license works submitted for analysis for training purposes without explicit permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors that ingest or license submitted stories as training data should be excluded. The editorial team should require explicit contractual guarantees that submitted material will not be used to train models absent clear permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect creatives' rights in vendor products
rubrics_metrics.description: Company is respectful of the rights of creatives in all of their products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess vendor policies for intellectual property, licensing, and rights management; prefer companies that foreground authors' rights and provide transparent data-handling policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detector accuracy including non-native English writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy, even with non-native English writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on validated accuracy across author demographics; avoid tools shown to misidentify works by non-native English writers. Review independent studies and run in-house validation on representative samples to measure false positive and false negative rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for common submission file formats (DOCX/RTF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has an API capable of supporting DOCX and RTF files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose detectors that accept the same file formats your submissions process uses to avoid forced conversions that might alter text or metadata. Prefer tools with an API for integration into editorial workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affordability for short fiction publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Affordable for a short fiction publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small magazines have limited budgets; evaluate cost per-API-call or subscription model and prefer solutions that are financially sustainable for low-volume, nonprofit, or small commercial publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt tools that prevent generated-text detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not sell a product that prevents generated text from being detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vendors whose business model includes obfuscation or 'undetectability' products. Such companies actively harm editorial integrity and may undermine the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tools with rampant false positives/false negatives and biased behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of the detectors we tested were extremely unreliable. False positives and false negatives were rampant and ... many of these products suffered from a tendency to misidentify works from non-native English language writers as AI generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject detection tools with poor reliability or documented demographic bias. Run your own tests, consult independent studies, and prioritize tools with transparent error metrics and mitigations for bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider provenance and ethics of detector training data
rubrics_metrics.description: The best quality detection requires the developer to use the output of unethically trained systems against it... it is, in a sense, the grandchild product of stolen data that has been turned against its parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the ethical trade-offs of using detectors trained on data obtained without proper consent. Even if a tool is effective, consider whether using it implicitly rewards or profits parties who exploited creators. Document ethical rationale for adopting or rejecting such tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer detectors that are replicable and help maintain open submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a detector (that meets my specifications) would significantly decrease the false positive rate, improve response times, and allow us to withstand a significant increase in volume... it would be replicable in a way that would help other editors maintain the open submissions practices that have made the short fiction community what it is today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tools that other small editors can realistically adopt (documentation, cost, integration), so that open submissions can be preserved across the field. Consider community-benefit and ease-of-adoption when evaluating solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve open submissions to protect new and underrepresented authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Open submissions level the playing field, creating opportunities for all authors regardless of how well-known they are to the staff. Should this path to publication close, it would disproportionately impact new authors and those from communities that are not typically represented...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policies should prioritize maintaining accessible submission pathways. When implementing filters or detectors, ensure they do not create barriers that disproportionately exclude new, marginalized, or international authors — build appeals and human-review paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational scalability and editor wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume is simply too high and the emotional toll of being suspicious all the time has its downsides too. Something has to change, preferably before things start to break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems (filters + tooling + staffing) to scale with submission volume and to reduce emotional/ cognitive load on staff. Use detection to reduce manual burden but keep humane processes to reduce constant suspicion and burnout.
